(p-٦٨٠)Sūrat "al-Fīl" (The Elephant)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ "Kayfa" (how) is in a position of accusative (naṣb) governed by "fa'ala" (dealt), not by "alam tara" (have you not considered), because of the meaning of interrogation (istifhām) contained in "kayfa." The clause takes the place of the two objects of "tara" (consider). In "alam tara" there is an expression of wonder (ta'jīb), meaning: Allah marvelled at His Prophet's disbelief in the Arabs, though this great sign of Allah's had been witnessed. The meaning is: you saw the traces of Allah's handiwork with the Abyssinians, and you heard the reports of it related through successive transmission (tawātur), so they stood for you in the place of direct witnessing.

﴿with the companions of the elephant﴾. It is related that Abraha ibn al-Sabbāḥ, king of Yemen, before Ashama al-Najāshī, built a church (kanīsa) in Ṣan'ā' and named it "al-Qullays," and he wished to divert the pilgrims toward it. A man from Kināna went out and sat in it at night, and this angered him. It is also said that a group of Arabs lit a fire, and the wind carried it and burned the church. So he swore that he would demolish the Ka'ba. He set out with the Abyssinians, and with him was an elephant named "Maḥmūd," which was strong and huge, and twelve other elephants besides it. When he reached Mughammas, 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib went out to him and offered him a third of the wealth of Tihāma in return for his turning back, but he refused. He arranged his army and sent the elephant forward. Whenever they directed it toward the Sacred Precinct (Ḥaram), it knelt down and would not move, and whenever they directed it toward Yemen, it ran hastily. Then Allah sent birds, each bird carrying a stone in its beak and two stones in its feet, larger than a lentil and smaller than a chickpea. The stone would fall upon a man's head and come out through his anus, and on every stone was the name of the one it would fall upon. So they fled and perished. Abraha did not die until his chest split open from his heart, and his vizier Abū Yaksūm escaped, with a bird circling above him, until he reached the Najāshī. He related the story to him, and when he finished it the stone fell upon him, and he dropped dead before his hands.

It is also related that Abraha had taken two hundred camels from 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib, so he went out to him on account of them. He was great in his eyes, for he was a tall and handsome man. It was said: this is the chief of Quraysh and the lord of the caravan of Makka, who feeds the people in the plain and the wild beasts on the mountain peaks. When he mentioned his need, Abraha said: you have fallen from my eyes. I came to demolish the House which is your religion and the religion of your forefathers and your honour since ancient times, and you are occupied with the herd of camels that was taken from you. 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib said: I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾

"In tadlil (in futility/loss), in tadyi' (waste) and ibtal (nullification). It is said: 'dallala kaydahu' (he made his plot go astray) when he made it lost and wasted. And al-Imru' al-Qays was called 'al-Malik al-Dillil' (the king who went astray), because he lost (dallala) his father's kingdom, i.e., wasted it. The meaning is that they first plotted against the House by building the Qulleys (a church), so that they might turn the faces of the pilgrims toward it; so He made their plot go astray by bringing fire upon it. Then they plotted against it a second time by intending to demolish it, so He made their plot go astray by sending birds upon them."
﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾, *hazāʾiq* (bundles), the singular of which is *ibbalah* (إبّالَةٌ). Al-Zajjaj said: groups from here and groups from there.

Qur'anic quotations in ﴿ ﴾ are kept with markers.

"Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 105, verse 4:"

﴿They pelt them﴾. Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) read: "yarmihim" (He pelts them), i.e., Allah, or: the birds, because it is a collective noun of masculine gender, and it is only made feminine according to meaning.

﴿with stones of sijjil﴾. It is a arabicized word (mu'arrab) from "sankil" (Persian: sang-gil), and the majority of scholars hold this view, i.e., baked clay (al-ajurr).
﴿So He made them like eaten straw﴾: a crop that worms had eaten.
